messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Children Present: Being around children, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Miguel had spent most of his adult life in courtrooms and county buildings, moving through them with the measured efficiency of a prosecutor who knew how to read a room. At 67, widowed and living alone, he still kept to routines that made him feel steady: early mornings, a precise commute, familiar offices, familiar faces. What changed was the assault itself, which had occurred in a place and at a moment that left him feeling stripped of the ordinary cues he relied on to judge safety. The details remained painfully clear to him. When he spoke about it, he did not have to search for the memory; it came with the force of something immediate, as if he were there again, and he described it in exact fragments, down to the sensations on his skin and the surrounding layout. The experience had involved a known person, someone connected enough to matter, which made later encounters with related people particularly loaded for him. He found that even seeing people with ties to that individual could pull him back into the event with alarming speed, not as an abstract recollection but as a living scene. He would feel his chest tighten and his attention narrow, and he knew the memory had arrived before he had any chance to push it away.

In the weeks and months after the assault, Miguel became increasingly preoccupied with danger in ordinary settings. He began avoiding unfamiliar places because he could not assess them quickly enough, and the effort of entering an unknown building left him tense and watchful. If he had to go somewhere new for work, he would hesitate at the doorway, looking for exits almost immediately, mapping routes out of the room before he had even settled into a chair. In court buildings, municipal offices, and waiting areas, his eyes moved automatically to doors, hallways, and corners. He also noticed potential weapons or dangerous objects wherever he went, not because he wanted to but because his attention kept snagging on things that could be used to harm someone: sharp edges, heavy objects, anything that might become dangerous in the wrong hands. This scanning became part of how he moved through his day, especially in professional settings where he had once felt competent and in control.

Certain triggers arrived with startling specificity. Being around children could bring the event sharply to mind, not because he believed they were in danger, but because their presence seemed to make the whole memory rise up in his body with the same suddenness it had when it first happened. He would notice himself becoming rigid and hyperaware in family gatherings, public spaces, or anywhere children were nearby. He was also troubled by a specific temperature on the skin. On some occasions, a particular coolness or warmth during bathing, changing clothes, or stepping into air-conditioned spaces seemed to land on him with the force of the assault’s bodily sensations, and he would freeze for a moment, feeling as though the present had folded into the past. He did not describe these moments as symbolic; to him they were direct reminders, proof that his body still recognized what had happened.

What haunted Miguel most was how vivid the memory remained. He said the images were clear and detailed in a way that offended him, as though the event had been etched into him. At times it did not feel like a completed event at all, but like something happening right now, intruding into whatever he was doing without warning. He could be in his office reviewing documents or standing in line at a coffee shop and suddenly find himself back in the scene, hearing and seeing it with an unwanted precision. He hated that it could force its way into his mind when he did not want it there. The intrusions left him feeling contaminated, and he used that word deliberately, speaking with quiet shame about feeling dirty because of what had been done to him. That sense of contamination sat alongside a broader conviction that the world was dangerous, a place where even familiarity could not be trusted. He had once believed his body could carry him through long days and demanding work without trouble, but now he was certain that it had been permanently damaged by what happened, not in a way anyone else could see, yet in a way he felt every time the memory surfaced or his skin encountered an unwelcome sensation.

As a widower, Miguel lived with the quietness of his home and the responsibilities of his job, but the assault had changed the way he moved through both. He took routes he knew well, declined invitations to new places, and positioned himself carefully in rooms so he could see entrances. At work, he could still perform, but the vigilance was exhausting and made him feel less present with colleagues. More recently, the combination of recurring memories, the relentless scanning, and the shame he carried about feeling contaminated made him realize he could no longer manage by sheer discipline alone. He came for help because he was tired of feeling as though he had to inspect every room, every person, and every sensation to stay safe. What he most feared was being pulled back into that moment without warning; what he most hoped for was some way to live in the world again without carrying the assault with him into every unfamiliar doorway, every encounter with children, and every change in the feel of his own skin.
